edits.text: As a last resort, when other principles are inconclusive, prefer a cut after the verb's immediately following core complement — i.e. after the end of the direct object, an essential prepositional phrase, or a clausal/infinitival complement — over a cut placed between the finite (main or light) verb and that complement.

As a last resort, prefer a cut after the end of an immediately following essential post‑nominal modifier (apposition, ‘named/called’ label, an ‘of’ PP, or a restrictive relative clause) over a cut positioned between the noun head and that modifier.

- As a last resort, prefer a cut after the main finite verb (or after its immediately following core complement: direct object, essential prepositional phrase, clausal/infinitival/‘that’ complement) over a cut immediately after a sentence‑initial fronted adjunct (temporal, locative, conditional, or parenthetical).

Keep a finite (conjugated) main or light verb together with the immediately following constituent that completes its predicate when there is no intervening comma or parenthesis — direct object NP, essential PP, or a 'that'/infinitival/clausal complement should stay bound to the verb.

Keep a noun head together with an immediately following essential post‑nominal modifier when the modifier immediately follows with no intervening comma (apposition, 'named/called' label, 'of' PP, or restrictive relative beginning with who/which/that).

Keep a sentence-initial fronted adjunct (temporal, locative, conditional, or parenthetical phrase) together with the finite main verb or the clause it scopes over (the verb/clause that appears later), i.e., bind the adjunct to its governing clause so its attachment and scope are preserved.

edits._was: - Does translating the two sides separately still allow a faithful reconstruction of the whole sentence? If an essential attachment or complement would be lost, cohesion is reduced.
